newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tycoon blames himself and banks for German scandal.
newsitem.headline: Tycoon blames himself and banks for German scandal.

text.p: Juergen Schneider, a property tycoon accused of fraud in Germany's biggest corporate scandal, said on Monday at the start of his trial that he was not "innocent as a lamb", but he insisted his bankers shared blame for the fiasco.

In an emotional statement read out to a packed court, Schneider, whose empire collapsed in 1994 under debt of more than five billion marks ($2.9 billion at current rates), said he had not been motivated by greed but by the dream of being able to give historic flair back to Germany's cities.
"This ambitous goal took hold of me more and more," said Schneider, who appeared tired. "Some people who know me will say I was possessed. I can hardly contradict that."

No longer wearing the toupe he sported in his heyday as one of the country's most feted entrepreneurs, Schneider, 63, spoke quietly for 45 minutes to the hushed court, peering up occasionally over his gold- rimmed spectacles.

The case has gripped Germany -- already inspiring a feature film -- and could further embarrass the country's big banks which have already suffered public ridicule at the ease with which they were alleged to have been fooled into doling out billions.
Hilmar Kopper, the former head of Deutsche Bank AG, Schneider's main creditor, made matters worse in 1994 by dismissing 50 million marks owed to Schneider's trade creditors as "peanuts".

Prosecutors have said they found no evidence to back Schneider's allegations that the banks were to blame but added that major mistakes were made. Schneider's lawyers plan to call bank officials into the witness stand during the trial.
Schneider could face up to 15 years in prison if found guilty.
Prosecutors allege Schneider, whose group invested in some of Germany's most prestigious real estate, fooled banks into extending credit by overstating rent income on properties and by forging bills.
Schneider said he did not contradict the prosecution's allegations regarding the loans. "But that in no way means that I submit myself to a guilty verdict," he added.
He admitted for the first time that he had presented expected rental income on properties as actual income when he asked banks to extend credit.
"As I told the Federal Criminal Police, I don't want to present myself as being innocent as a lamb here, I'm not."
But he added that the banks shared responsibility because they had bankrolled a business they knew to be highly speculative. That had to be taken into account in arriving at a fair verdict.
He had also assumed that the banks deliberately ignored the irregularities in his loan requests because they shared his conviction the projects would be profitable in the future.

"I was guided by how the individual properties would stand in the market in five or six years' time. My view went into the future. The banks knew that and still they appeared to finance the present in their documentation."

Citing three cases in which he obtained funds from Deutsche Bank AG, Dresdner Bank AG and Deutsche Bau - und Bodenbank, Schneider said he had interpreted their lack of rigorous checks as "silent agreement to undertake project financing without making this clear in their records".
Part of the reason for this, Schneider alleged, was that the banks were bound by German property credit rules which forced them to treat what was in effect project finance as standard property loans.
"I assumed this required cosmetic measures," he said.

Speaking in a mild local accent, the Frankfurt boy made good who financed his university education by working as a bricklayer said he was proud of what he had achieved in his 40 years in the business.

"I told police that I described the...buildings as 'my children'. That was not really a joke. I admit that I still have a very emotional relationship with my projects with a good portion of pride, even though I lost the properties long ago."
The collapse in 1994 sparked fears of a German real estate slump, left hundreds of small craftsmen fighting for their livelihoods and exposed his banks to public outrage.
The Schneider group filed for bankruptcy shortly after he and his wife Claudia disappeared. They were arrested in Miami one year later and extradited to Germany in 1996.
The tycoon gained fame by refurbishing historic hotels and stylish shopping malls in the post-unification property boom, adding flair to cities up and down the country.
But his facade crumbled as his rent income was too low to repay his debts, causing the group to slide towards bankruptcy. ($ = 1.739 German Marks)
